principles.text: Don't chase gap-ups: avoid buying opening range highs or first-15-minute strength; skip the first 15 minutes after the open.
The highest-quality pullback buy is at the rising weekly 9 EMA — be patient and wait for price to actually reach it instead of entering early; entering too early gets you stopped on the flush.
A stock gapping up 20% right after stopping you out is part of the game — it could just as easily have gapped down. Follow the stop, take the exit, and move on to the next trade without regret.
When indices look weak but leading stocks are pulling back into rising EMAs, that is a buy-weakness environment — not a reason to short or sell positions.
A quick intraday flush against a strong primary uptrend is a countertrend move: probability and risk/reward favor pullback buys and bounce plays over shorts.

Buying off the lows below the lower-timeframe EMAs is a lower-win-rate entry but catches fast movers; waiting for price to reclaim and hold above all EMAs is safer but risks missing the move. Know which trade-off you're taking.
You don't need to wait for a daily reclaim of an EMA or support level: if a stock is genuinely finding support, a 5-minute candle breakout off the low is a valid entry with a tighter stop.

Risk management is the number one objective, above everything else: set the stop and define your risk before you enter, and never widen a stop after entry. Entry and exit tactics can evolve; this never changes.
Cap total portfolio open risk: even when multiple valid setups fire the same day, stop adding new positions once open risk is too heavy (he skipped Marvell after five new buys).

To fix overtrading, review your past trades to find the nonsense ones and identify the specific conditions where you overtrade (extended markets, choppy periods) — then deliberately reduce trade count in those conditions.
Treat trend lines as zones, not magic lines — they're too subjective to anchor decisions on. Keep charts clean; use them only as secondary confluence for pullback buys.
Hold through earnings only with enough cushion above your stop (e.g. ~8%); if the stock closes weak near the stop into the report, exit before earnings instead.

As the account grows, split an entry into tranches like a big fund would (e.g. thirds: first pullback, next pullback, breakout day) — 0.3% trade risk becomes ~0.1% per tranche, keeping cost basis low and drawdowns small.

Match risk-per-trade to your system's win rate: a low-win-rate, tight-stop approach is prone to losing streaks and should risk small (~0.3%); a wider-stop, higher-win-rate approach can justify larger risk per trade.
Let the stop decide what you do — no second-guessing, no daily-drawdown overrides; let the market do its own thing.

If a position is far from its stop, don't watch it — the stop takes care of the position (even while traveling). Stay up for the close only on special events: earnings on a holding, FOMC, unusually volatile days.
Trade liquid stocks so you can use market orders and get in fast on trigger; reserve limit orders for thin or wide-spread names to control slippage.
